title: Three reasons your GROUP BY total never matches the dashboard
course: Why your GROUP BY total doesn't match the dashboard

events.narration: Hey, if you're a data analyst who writes S-Q-L every day and you've ever had that stomach-dropping moment where your GROUP BY total doesn't match the dashboard, this lesson's for you. By the end, you'll be able to spot and fix the three sneakiest reasons your numbers disagree: fan-out joins inflating your rows, hidden dashboard filters quietly excluding data, and metric definitions that drifted apart when nobody was looking. Let's get into it.

Here's what we're working with. Two tables. First, we've got the orders table, with columns for order ID, region, order date, and order total. Then there's the order items table, which has item ID, order ID, product name, line item price, quantity, and discount. Classic one-to-many setup, right? One order, multiple line items. And that relationship is exactly where our first trap is hiding.

Alright, here's the query that gets everyone in trouble. We're joining orders to order items and then doing a GROUP BY on region, summing order total, and counting rows. Seems totally reasonable, right? But here's the problem. When you join orders to order items, every order row gets duplicated once per line item. So if an order has three line items, that order total gets summed three times. Let's run it and see the damage.

Look at this. The West region shows eight rows and an inflated revenue of two thousand two hundred forty-one point seven three. East has six rows coming in at one thousand four hundred ninety-five point four zero. And Central shows four rows at five hundred seventy-two point four zero. Those row counts are way too high, and those revenue numbers are bloated. That's our fan-out in action, every order total getting counted once per line item.

Now here's the fix. Instead of joining and summing blindly, we pre-aggregate the orders in a subquery first, then join to order items separately. This way each order total only gets counted once, and we pick up the line item count on its own. Let's run this corrected version.

Now we're talking. The West region has three orders, true revenue of seven hundred seventy-seven point two four, and eight line items. East shows three orders, seven hundred forty-seven point seven zero in true revenue, six line items. Central has two orders at two hundred fifty-five point six zero with four line items. See how the order counts dropped way down compared to those inflated row counts from before? West went from eight rows to three actual orders. That's the fan-out completely gone. Your row counts are your best friend when debugging this stuff.

Let's just appreciate the difference side by side for a second. West's inflated revenue was two thousand two hundred forty-one point seven three. The real number? Seven hundred seventy-seven point two four. That's nearly three times too high. If you'd put that inflated number in a report, you'd have some very confused stakeholders. Fan-out joins are sneaky because the query runs fine, no errors, no warnings, just quietly wrong numbers. Always check your row counts before and after a join.

Okay, fan-out's fixed, filters are matched, but there's one more gremlin. Culprit three is metric definition drift, and it's the most annoying one because everyone thinks they're calculating "revenue" but nobody agreed on what revenue actually means. This first query sums the order total column from the orders table. That's one definition of revenue. Let's see what it gives us.

Using order total, we get Central at two hundred fifty-five point six zero, East at seven hundred forty-seven point seven zero, and West at seven hundred seventy-seven point two four. These are the gross order totals. Now let's see what happens when we calculate revenue the way a dashboard might.

This second query calculates revenue from the order items table instead, using line item price times quantity minus the discount. That's net revenue after discounts, a totally different animal. If your dashboard's using this formula but you're summing order total, you'll never match. Let's run it and see the gap.

There it is. Revenue from line items gives us Central at two hundred three point three zero, East at four hundred eighty-two point zero four, and West at five hundred twenty-three point eight six. Compare that to the order total numbers we just saw. East dropped from seven hundred forty-seven point seven zero down to four hundred eighty-two point zero four. That's a big gap, and it's entirely because discounts are being subtracted in one formula but not the other. Neither number is wrong, they're just answering different questions. The fix is simple: find out which formula your dashboard uses and match it exactly in your S-Q-L.

Alright, here's your thirty-second debug checklist for every time your numbers don't match the dashboard. Step one, check for fan-out. Compare row counts before and after your joins. If they jump, you've got duplicates inflating your totals. Step two, match every dashboard filter in your WHERE clause, date ranges, status exclusions, test accounts, all of it. Step three, confirm the metric formula. Is the dashboard using order total or line item price times quantity minus discount? They're not the same thing. Do these three checks in order, every time, and you'll stop chasing phantom mismatches. Grab the exercise files linked in the description and try it yourself.
